Quidra.probe_status: DBG-1 IS NOT EXPRESSIBLE IN QUIDRA 0.2.0. The frozen probe requires a dynamic array of 3 aggregates and a function that loops over the array reading their fields. Quidra 0.2.0's definite-initialization checker rejects every read of a field of a class value held in an array. Nine distinct formulations were attempted (direct index, for-in by value, for-in by writable reference `for &item in items`, reference binding to an element, copy of an element into a local, class value passed by value to a function, writable-reference array parameter, union conversion + exhaustive match, and a method call on the element). All were rejected. Q1-Q4 therefore could not be executed against DBG-1 itself; a supplementary Quidra program was built to establish whether the failures are probe artefacts or real capability gaps, and it confirmed they are real capability gaps.

Quidra.reasoning: Exactly one of Q1-Q6 is satisfied (Q5), so the level is 'None' (0 or 1 of Q1-Q6), score 0. Not the level above (Minimal, 20) because that requires exactly 2 satisfied indicators and only Q5 is satisfied; there is no lower level. The score does not rest on the probe being inexpressible: a supplementary Quidra program that Quidra 0.2.0 CAN compile was built with the documented `--debug` flag and independently confirms each failure. That executable contains no DWARF sections, no Mach-O debug map and an empty .dSYM (Q1); lldb cannot resolve any source-line breakpoint against it, and a breakpoint forced onto the mangled native symbol `n_accumulate` stops the process but yields no named locals whatsoever (Q2, Q3). Quidra's own README states the position exactly: it guarantees native function/symbol visibility and does not yet claim source-line DWARF mapping. No CPU profiler is shipped or documented (Q4) and no DAP or editor-debugging integration is published (Q6). Q5 is awarded on the literal text of the indicator -- AddressSanitizer is a memory analysis tool and it is named in Quidra's official documentation as being applied to generated native programs -- although, unlike the named tool for each of the other nine languages, it is described as a development/CI build configuration of the Quidra project rather than a documented user-invocable option; scoring Q5 unsatisfied on a stricter reading would leave the level and score unchanged at None/0.

cross_language_consistency_note:
Four decisions were fixed once and applied identically to all ten languages, and all four were settled while only the nine established languages had been examined -- Quidra was collected last, exactly as global_rules.evidence_collection_order requires, so no rule here could have been shaped by Quidra's result.

(1) BREAKPOINT LINE. The frozen dbg1_debugger recipes leave the breakpoint line as the placeholder <L>, 'read off the probe source at run time'. Two structurally-defined lines are used for every language: L_loop, the outer-loop statement line inside the function that loops over the array (where the array is a parameter, hence a frame local), and L_call, the call-site line in the entry point (where the array has just been built). Every language was run at both; Q2 and Q3 are satisfied if the required rendering occurs in either session. This rule is outcome-independent -- both lines are read off the source structure, not chosen after seeing results -- and it matters because three frozen build cells (C++ -O2, Rust -O, Swift -O) specify optimizing flags, so variable liveness inside a hot loop measures the optimizer rather than the debugger. Under a single-line rule Swift would have scored 40 and Rust 60 purely because of where the optimizer happened to keep a register live, which is not what Q2 and Q3 are written to test.

(2) WHAT COUNTS AS Q3 RENDERING. Uniform standard: the debugger must display the aggregate's fields BY NAME as language-level values, AND display at least one element of the dynamic array as a language-level value with its field names, using the debugger's own variable/expression command with at most one documented field or index step. C++, Rust and Swift expand automatically; Java and Kotlin need `dump items.elementData[0]`; Zig needs `items.ptr[0]`; Python needs `p vars(item)` / `p items[2].name`; TypeScript needs `exec items[0]`. The same single step was allowed to all of them, so no language was failed for a formatter convenience another language happened to ship. Quidra fails Q3 not by this margin but absolutely: no named variable of any kind is visible.

(3) macOS DWARF PACKAGING. On this host DWARF lives in the object files and the executable carries only a debug map, so `dwarfdump` on the executable alone is empty for C++, Rust, Swift and Zig. One identical remedy was applied to all four: retain the intermediate object with the toolchain's documented flag (-save-temps / -C save-temps) where the driver deletes it, then run `xcrun dsymutil` exactly as the frozen cells already direct for C++, Rust and Swift. Go was NOT given this remedy because it does not need it -- it embeds DWARF directly, compressed, in __zdebug_* sections, which Apple dwarfdump cannot decompress, so Go's DWARF was read with Go's own debug/macho + debug/dwarf. The SAME dsymutil step was then applied to Quidra, and Quidra's executable turned out to contain no DWARF, no debug-map entries and an empty .dSYM -- so Quidra's Q1 failure is a measured absence under the same procedure that succeeded for four other native languages, not a packaging artefact.

(4) Q4 AND Q5 ADMISSIBILITY. Q4 and Q5 turn on 'shipped with the toolchain OR named in the language's official documentation', judged against the frozen official_docs_root for each language. For every language the toolchain's own subcommand list was enumerated on this host before consulting documentation, so 'shipped' was measured rather than assumed. Apple's Instruments/xctrace is admissible for C++ and Swift only because Apple is a frozen member of those two languages' official_project_set; it was NOT credited to Rust or Zig, whose official project sets do not include Apple and whose own documentation names no profiler that runs on macOS/arm64. That is precisely why Rust and Zig sit at 80 rather than 100, and it is a property of the frozen table, not a judgement made here.

CONSISTENCY CHECK PERFORMED. The ten assignments were re-read together. No two languages with the same observable evidence received different levels: Java and Kotlin have identical evidence on Q1-Q4 and both score 100; Rust and Zig fail only Q4, for the same reason, and both score 80; the six languages at 100 each satisfy all six indicators on directly-executed evidence. No two languages with clearly different evidence received the same level: Go is separated from the 80s by the total absence of any usable debugger session on this host, and Quidra is separated from every other language by the absence of source-level debug information altogether.
limitations: GO'S SCORE IS SUBSTANTIALLY A HOST ARTEFACT, AND THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT CAVEAT IN THIS METRIC. Go loses both Q2 and Q3 -- 40 points -- solely because Delve is not installed on this host and global_rules.host_verification.no_installation_of_extra_software forbids installing it. Delve is admissible (go.dev/doc/diagnostics names it), it is the debugger the Go project's own VS Code extension drives over DAP, and Go's toolchain is otherwise complete. Per global_rules.tool_availability_states this is state S3, the indicator is recorded NOT SATISFIED with verification_status=unverified, and the loss MUST be published in standard/rubrics/host_limited_indicators.json, which must also carry the frozen disclosure sentence that Quidra's toolchain was built from source on this host and so cannot lose any indicator for a repackaging reason.

THE FROZEN dbg1_debug_build CELLS FOR C++, RUST AND SWIFT SPECIFY OPTIMIZING FLAGS (-O2, -O, -O) WHILE GO'S DISABLES OPTIMIZATION (-N -l) AND ZIG'S IS -ODebug. This is an internal inconsistency in the frozen recipe table: a cell named 'debug build' that optimizes. It does not change any score as computed here, because the two-line rule in cross_language_consistency_note(1) removes the dependence on optimizer liveness, but an auditor applying a single-breakpoint-line reading of the same frozen cells would obtain Swift 40 and Rust 60. Every session at both lines is retained in standard/rubrics/logs/dbg/ so either reading can be recomputed without re-running anything.

TWO FROZEN VERIFICATION COMMANDS DID NOT EMIT WHAT THEIR INDICATOR ASKS FOR AND WERE MINIMALLY ADJUSTED, WITH THE ADJUSTMENT RECORDED. (a) `javap -l` warns 'option -l without -c, line number and local variable tables will not be printed'; -c was added for Java and Kotlin alike. (b) The dsymutil step in the C++/Rust/Swift cells fails when the compiler driver deletes the intermediate object, so -save-temps / -C save-temps was added for those three and dsymutil was additionally run for Zig and Quidra, which are in the same macOS debug-map situation. Both adjustments are conditional, language-neutral and were applied to every language in the same position. Neither adds a capability: they only let the named tool print what the frozen cell already asked it to print.

DBG-1 IS NOT EXPRESSIBLE IN QUIDRA 0.2.0, so Quidra's Q1-Q4 could not be executed against the frozen probe. Quidra's definite-initialization checker rejects every read of a field of a class value held in an array; nine formulations were attempted and all were rejected, and the checker source (src/checker.cpp, initialized_paths_for_expr) confirms initialization paths are tracked only for NameExpr and MemberExpr, never for an index expression or a for-in loop variable of class element type. A supplementary Quidra program within what the language can express was therefore built and debugged under the identical procedure; it independently confirms no DWARF, no source-line breakpoints and no named locals. Quidra's 0 does not depend on the probe being blocked. NOTE FOR THE FUNCTIONALITY / EXPRESSIVENESS AND DIAGNOSTICS SCORERS: the array-of-class-field-read limitation is a language-capability finding surfaced here and may be independently relevant to those metrics.

QUIDRA'S Q5 IS THE ONE INDICATOR IN THIS METRIC AWARDED ON A LITERAL READING THAT AN AUDITOR MIGHT TIGHTEN. AddressSanitizer is named in Quidra's official documentation as being propagated to generated native programs, which satisfies Q5 as written; but unlike the tool named for each of the other nine languages, it is described as a development/CI build configuration of the Quidra project rather than a user-invocable option, and `quidra --help` exposes no sanitizer flag. Scoring Q5 unsatisfied would leave Quidra at level None / 0 regardless, so the reading does not affect the result.

PROBE SOURCES WERE REPAIRED WHERE THEY DID NOT BUILD OR DID NOT MEET THE FROZEN PROBE REQUIREMENT, BEFORE ANY SCORING. The Zig probe used std.heap.GeneralPurposeAllocator, std.ArrayList(Item){} and std.fs.File.stdout(), none of which exist in Zig 0.16.0; it was updated to DebugAllocator, .empty and std.debug.print. The Python probe ran only 0.58 s, below DBG-1's frozen '>= 2 seconds of CPU time' requirement, and its iteration count was raised until it did (2.20 s). Every language's probe was timed and every one now meets the >= 2 s requirement. The five compiled languages that share an iteration count (C++, Rust, Go, Swift, Zig) all print checksum=797031483, and Java and Kotlin agree with them, which cross-validates the probe sources against each other.

AN EARLIER PASS OF PYTHON EVIDENCE WAS COLLECTED UNDER /usr/bin/python3 (3.9.6) RATHER THAN THE FROZEN 3.14.5, AND WAS DISCARDED. Every Python figure reported here was re-collected with /opt/homebrew/bin/python3.14 and the interpreter version is recorded inside the evidence excerpt. Java and Kotlin evidence likewise required /opt/homebrew/opt/openjdk/bin on PATH, because /usr/bin/javac on this host is the macOS stub that reports no Java runtime; javac -version was confirmed as 26.0.1, matching environment.json.

PYTHON'S Q1 AND Q6 REST ON THE BROADEST ADMISSIBLE READINGS AND ARE FLAGGED FOR AUDIT. Q1 uses the .pyc code-object line/position/local-name tables as the 'equivalent documented format', which is the citation path the frozen Python recipe cell explicitly invites, and which is the same category of evidence that satisfies Q1 for Java and Kotlin. Q6 uses IDLE's editor-integrated debugger plus the PEP 768 attach interface, because the mainstream Python DAP implementation (microsoft/debugpy) is published by Microsoft, which is NOT a member of Python's frozen official_project_set and therefore cannot satisfy Q6's publisher test. If an auditor rejects the Q6 reading, Python falls to 5/80 alongside Rust and Zig; if the Q1 reading is also rejected, Python falls to 4/60.

TYPESCRIPT'S Q2/Q3 SESSION IS ON THE EMITTED JAVASCRIPT, NOT THE .ts SOURCE, because the frozen dbg1_debugger cell directs `node inspect` at build/dbg1.js and node inspect resolves breakpoints on the generated file rather than consuming the source map that Q1 credits. The indicator says 'a source line of DBG-1' and the JavaScript is the artifact the frozen recipe debugs, so it is scored satisfied; an auditor requiring the breakpoint to land on the .ts line would need a DAP client (vscode-js-debug), which is not runnable headless on this host.

NO INDICATOR IN THIS METRIC WAS SCORED FROM REPUTATION OR MEMORY. Every Q1-Q4 result is a command executed on this host with its output captured in standard/rubrics/logs/dbg/ and standard/rubrics/build/; every Q5 and Q6 result carries an exact URL, an accession timestamp and a verbatim excerpt.
